system:
You are the analysis agent of a reporting platform for Australia's threatened species. Conservation practitioners — people in government agencies, NGOs and recovery teams who decide where to survey, what to protect and what to escalate — read what you produce. You have read-only SQL access to the platform's database and produce insights from it, each grounded in queries you ran.

# The data

PostgreSQL 17 with PostGIS 3.5. The corpus is every occurrence record the Atlas of Living Australia (ALA) tags as nationally threatened (EPBC Critically Endangered, Endangered or Vulnerable), observed January 2015 to 2026-09-30, from one bulk download (DOI 10.26197/ala.40eee344-07ce-48d2-9ec2-be39574ff4c7): about 2.1 million records, 1,850 taxa, 300+ contributing datasets. Alongside it are all-taxa effort counts per 0.1° cell per month for the same period.

corpus.analysable_occurrences — VIEW — the records to analyse: occurrences that are valid, dated, and not from telemetry (animal-tracking) datasets. Includes dataset_kind ('wild' or 'managed'). Prefer this over occurrences.
  columns: record_id text, source text, source_record_id text, occurrence_id text, harvest_id text, snapshot_page text, fetched_at timestamp with time zone, data_resource_uid text, license text, taxon_concept_id text, scientific_name text, vernacular_name text, national_status text, event_date timestamp with time zone, first_loaded_at timestamp with time zone, decimal_latitude double precision, decimal_longitude double precision, coordinate_uncertainty_m double precision, state_province text, ibra_region text, locality text, geom USER-DEFINED, basis_of_record text, individual_count integer, recorded_by_pseudonym text, occurrence_remarks text, event_remarks text, source_assertions ARRAY, is_valid boolean, issue_count integer, cell_lat numeric, cell_lon numeric, dataset_kind text

corpus.datasets — TABLE — contributing datasets; kind is 'wild', 'managed' (fenced havens, reintroductions) or 'telemetry' (excluded from analysable_occurrences).
  columns: data_resource_uid text, name text, kind text, kind_reason text, first_seen_at timestamp with time zone

corpus.effort_cells — TABLE — ALL-taxa record counts (threatened or not, telemetry excluded) per 0.1° cell per month: the denominator for reporting rates. Join on cell_lat/cell_lon and month.
  columns: cell_lat numeric, cell_lon numeric, period_start date, period_end date, records integer, harvest_id text

corpus.harvest_runs — TABLE — provenance of each harvest (the corpus download and the effort counts).
  columns: harvest_id text, harvest_key text, run_id text, source text, description text, query jsonb, started_at timestamp with time zone, finished_at timestamp with time zone, expected_records integer, retrieved_records integer, complete boolean, corpus_hash text, request_count integer, warnings jsonb, analysis jsonb, loaded_at timestamp with time zone

corpus.occurrences — TABLE — every canonical occurrence record, telemetry included. geom is a PostGIS Point (SRID 4326); cell_lat/cell_lon are the 0.1° grid cell (rounded to nearest, as ALA assigns them).
  columns: record_id text, source text, source_record_id text, occurrence_id text, harvest_id text, snapshot_page text, fetched_at timestamp with time zone, data_resource_uid text, license text, taxon_concept_id text, scientific_name text, vernacular_name text, national_status text, event_date timestamp with time zone, first_loaded_at timestamp with time zone, decimal_latitude double precision, decimal_longitude double precision, coordinate_uncertainty_m double precision, state_province text, ibra_region text, locality text, geom USER-DEFINED, basis_of_record text, individual_count integer, recorded_by_pseudonym text, occurrence_remarks text, event_remarks text, source_assertions ARRAY, is_valid boolean, issue_count integer, cell_lat numeric, cell_lon numeric

corpus.taxa — TABLE — one row per taxon (key taxon_concept_id); national_status is the EPBC status ALA attached.
  columns: taxon_concept_id text, scientific_name text, vernacular_name text, taxon_rank text, kingdom text, phylum text, taxon_class text, taxon_order text, family text, genus text, national_status text, status_seen_at timestamp with time zone

corpus.taxon_tiers — VIEW — per taxon: analysable records since 2015, last record date, and statistical_tier (≥100 records since 2015).
  columns: taxon_concept_id text, scientific_name text, vernacular_name text, national_status text, records_since_2015 bigint, last_record_at timestamp with time zone, statistical_tier boolean

Useful facts: EPSG:3577 (Australian Albers, equal-area, metres) is available for gridding and areas; ibra_region is the IBRA 7 bioregion (null offshore — IBRA covers land only); coordinate_uncertainty_m is the radius the true position may lie within.

# Known properties of this data — read before interpreting anything

- **Records measure effort as much as animals.** These are mostly opportunistic records. All-taxa recording roughly doubled between 2017–19 and 2022–24 (about 1.9×), so counts and range measures grow with effort. Use corpus.effort_cells as a denominator where it matters.
- **Recent months are incomplete.** Datasets reach ALA months to a year late: January–August 2026 holds about 20% of the records January–August 2024 holds, and eBird (the largest dataset) has not loaded 2026 at all. A recent decline is not evidence of anything until this is accounted for.
- **Sources start and stop.** A compilation that ends in 2020, or a targeted survey wound up inside an ongoing state atlas, looks exactly like range loss. Check which datasets carry a taxon's records in each period before calling a change real.
- **Locations vary in precision.** About half the analysable records are located to within 2 km; about a third state no uncertainty; ALA generalises many sensitive species to roughly 10 km.
- **Managed populations** (dataset_kind = 'managed', e.g. fenced havens and reintroductions) are in the analysable view and are not wild trend.
- **National status** is as ALA attached it. Never infer, change or second-guess a taxon's conservation status.
- Taxonomy can shift: a taxon "disappearing" from a region can be a name re-assignment.

# How to work

- Call run_sql with one SELECT (or WITH … SELECT) per call, no trailing statements. Results are capped at 200 rows and queries time out after 30 s, so aggregate in SQL rather than pulling rows. Each call returns a query_id.
- Record each insight with record_insight as soon as it is established. Every insight cites the query_ids whose results support it, and every number in it must be a value those queries returned or simple arithmetic on them. Do not state figures you did not query.
- taxon_concept_id must be copied exactly from corpus.taxa; region is an IBRA region name exactly as in ibra_region, or null for a national insight; period_start and period_end are the window the insight describes.
- Say how confident you are and why, in the confidence field: record counts, the datasets involved, effort, precision, and any artefact that could explain the pattern.
- When you have recorded everything worth recording, stop.

messages.content:
Report month: 2026-09 (2026-09-01 to 2026-09-30). Compute the three insights below exactly as defined and record them with record_insight, using the insight_type given. "Analysable" means corpus.analysable_occurrences. The statistical tier is taxa with statistical_tier = true in corpus.taxon_tiers.

## 1. silent_species — period 2023-10-01 to 2026-09-30
(a) Silent: taxa in corpus.taxa with no analysable record in that window (whatever their record count).
(b) Evidence gap: taxa with fewer than 10 analysable records since 2015.
(c) Regional silence: a taxon and IBRA region where the taxon had at least 5 analysable records in 2015–2019 but none in the window, while the taxon was still recorded nationally in the window.
Record one headline insight per kind (taxon and region null; figures {kind: "silent" | "evidence_gap" | "regional_silence", count}), then individual insights for the most important cases, up to 15 per kind (figures {kind, last_record_date, records_since_2015, …}; regional ones with region set).

## 2. range_change — statistical tier, 2017–2019 against 2022–2024 (period 2022-01-01 to 2024-12-31)
Per taxon and window, from analysable records with coordinates:
- AOO 10 km: distinct 10 km cells on an EPSG:3577 grid, all records; area = cells × 100 km².
- AOO 2 km: distinct 2 km cells, only records with coordinate_uncertainty_m ≤ 2000; area = cells × 4 km².
- EOO: area of the convex hull of all records, km².
Flag "contraction" or "expansion" when the 10 km AOO changes by at least 30% and both windows have at least 20 records.
Record headline insights with the count of contractions and of expansions (figures {flag, count}), then individual insights for the most important flagged taxa, up to 15 (figures {flag, aoo_10km_km2: {baseline, recent, change}, aoo_2km_km2: {baseline, recent, change}, eoo_km2: {baseline, recent, change}, records: {baseline, recent}}, change as a fraction).

## 3. notable_record — records in 2026-09 of statistical-tier taxa
A record is notable if it is more than 100 km from every earlier analysable record of the taxon (since 2015), or in an IBRA region with no earlier record of the taxon, or in a calendar month holding less than 1% of the taxon's 2015–2019 records (judged only where the taxon has at least 100 such records). Group by taxon and IBRA region: one insight per group, up to 30 (figures {reasons: [...], records, max_distance_to_prior_km}).

Beyond these, record anything else a practitioner should know as insight_type "other".

input.sql:
WITH w AS (SELECT taxon_concept_id, count(*) n FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences WHERE event_date >= '2023-10-01' AND event_date < '2026-10-01' GROUP BY 1),
a AS (SELECT taxon_concept_id, count(*) n, max(event_date) last FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences WHERE event_date >= '2015-01-01' GROUP BY 1)
SELECT count(*) total_taxa,
 count(*) FILTER (WHERE w.n IS NULL) silent,
 count(*) FILTER (WHERE coalesce(a.n,0) < 10) evidence_gap,
 count(*) FILTER (WHERE a.n IS NULL) zero_analysable,
 count(*) FILTER (WHERE w.n IS NULL AND a.n IS NULL) silent_zero
FROM corpus.taxa t LEFT JOIN w USING (taxon_concept_id) LEFT JOIN a USING (taxon_concept_id)
input.purpose: Headline counts for silent and evidence-gap taxa

  (array_agg(data_resource_uid ORDER BY event_date DESC))[1] last_ds

input.summary: Black-footed tree-rat (Mesembriomys gouldii gouldii, Endangered): 2,935 records 2015–2020, none since 28 Oct 2020, all from Fauna Atlas N.T. Ask NT agencies whether surveys after 2020 exist but are unshared, or whether monitoring stopped.

confidence.notes: Records come from Flora Atlas N.T. (dr362) and the NT Herbarium AVH feed (dr15866). Both supply records through 2026, so the source has not stopped. However, 796 of the 920 records are from one 2022 survey pulse, and Typhonium is a geophyte visible only in the wet season, so silence may just mean no targeted survey since.

input.summary: Typhonium mirabile (Endangered): 920 records since 2015 (796 in 2022), none since 1 Apr 2022, even though its NT flora sources are still active. It needs a wet-season resurvey to confirm the known populations are still there.

confidence.notes: Records come from NSW BioNet (dr368, active to 2026-09) and the NSW AVH feed. Records fell from 536 (2018) to 7 (2022), which looks like counts from survey programmes winding down rather than opportunistic recording. Related subspecies (corangensis, oblonga) still appear in the window, so a name re-assignment is worth checking.

input.summary: Callitris oblonga subsp. parva (Critically Endangered): 788 records since 2015, falling to 7 in 2022, none since 20 Sep 2022, although NSW BioNet is still active. Check with the NSW Saving our Species program whether monitoring continues.

confidence.notes: All records come from two research compilations that stopped: NESP MBH A1 elasmobranch fishing database (ends 2019-12-01) and NESP A12 northern threatened species (ends 2020-10). The silence is almost certainly the sources ending, not the shark disappearing.

input.summary: Northern river shark (Glyphis garricki, Endangered): 650 records, none since 1 Dec 2019. Every record came from NESP research compilations that ended in 2019–2020, so after 2020 the data hold nothing on this shark rather than evidence of loss. Current survey data need to be sourced.

confidence.notes: Records come from NT flora sources (dr362, dr15866) that remain active. They arrived in survey pulses (2018, 2021), a pattern that suggests targeted surveys. Wet-season geophyte.

input.summary: Typhonium jonesii (Endangered): 631 records in survey pulses in 2018 and 2021, none since 21 Feb 2021, although NT flora sources are still active. It is a candidate for a wet-season follow-up survey.

confidence.notes: Nearly all records come from Fauna Atlas N.T. (dr361, ends 2024-03), with 3 from the NT Museum OZCAM feed (dr343, ends 2022-12). Silent for nearly 8 years, which predates both sources stopping.

input.summary: Melville Island black-footed tree-rat (Mesembriomys gouldii melvillensis, Vulnerable): 254 records in 2016–2018, none since 7 Nov 2018. Ask Tiwi Islands programmes for any survey data after 2018.

confidence.notes: One source only (Fauna Atlas N.T., dr361), all from 2016–2017 survey work. Silent since mid-2017, long before the source stopped in 2024-03.

input.summary: Carpentarian rock-rat (Zyzomys palatalis, Endangered): 163 records in 2016–2017, none since 23 Jul 2017. This is the longest silence among well-recorded mammals and needs an urgent check against NT and recovery-team data.

confidence.notes: Recorded steadily (10–27 records a year, 2016–2022) by 4 sources including NSW BioNet and iNaturalist, both still active. A steady series that then stops is more informative than a one-off survey pulse ending.

input.summary: Illawarra Irene (Irenepharsus trypherus, Endangered): recorded every year 2016–2022 (134 records, 4 sources), then nothing since 21 Jan 2022, although its main sources are still active. This is the clearest case of a recording series breaking, so prioritise a site check.

confidence.notes: Almost entirely one 2021 survey pulse (132 records) in NSW BioNet plus iNaturalist. Silence most likely reflects no repeat survey.

input.summary: Cyphanthera scabrella (Endangered): 133 records, almost all from a 2021 survey, none since 25 Jan 2022. A repeat survey of the 2021 sites would settle its status.

confidence.notes: Last record falls just 18 days before the window opens; 7 sources, mostly herbaria and BioNet. Herbarium (AVH) feeds lag, so it may well be re-recorded once data arrive. Watch rather than escalate.

input.summary: Pokolbin mallee (Eucalyptus pumila, Vulnerable): 131 records from 7 sources, last on 13 Sep 2023, just before the window. It is probably a lag case, but if no record has appeared by the next report, ask Hunter Valley land managers for site data.

confidence.notes: All records come from finished research datasets: an eDNA survey (2017–2018), the NESP MBH A1 elasmobranch database (ends 2019) and NESP A12 (ends 2020). The silence comes from sources ending.

input.summary: Dwarf sawfish (Pristis clavata, Vulnerable): 93 records, none since 12 Sep 2018, all from research projects that have ended. No current data flow into ALA for this sawfish, which is a monitoring gap to fill.

confidence.notes: Recorded in 8 separate years by 4 sources including NSW BioNet and iNaturalist, both still active. A long series that then stops.

input.summary: Dwarf heath casuarina (Allocasuarina defungens, Endangered): 81 records over 8 years, none since 9 Jan 2023, although its sources are still active. A site check is worthwhile.

confidence.notes: Single source (NSW BioNet, still active); silent for about 3 years.

input.summary: Leptospermum petraeum (Critically Endangered): 70 BioNet records across 4 years, none since 18 Jun 2023. Ask the NSW program for monitoring results.

confidence.notes: Recorded in 7 years by the Victorian Biodiversity Atlas, Museums Victoria and iNaturalist. VBA has records only to 2026-06, so recent months are incomplete, but the gap is now more than 3 years.

input.summary: Dargo galaxias (Galaxias mungadhan, Critically Endangered): 47 records over 7 years, none since 3 May 2023. Check Victorian fish monitoring for later surveys.

confidence.notes: Recorded by 4 independent sources, including birdwatcher platforms (Birdata, NT WildWatch). Bird recording effort rose about 1.9× over the period, which makes the absence more meaningful. Small numbers, though. eBird records run only to 2025-08.

input.summary: Alligator Rivers yellow chat (Epthianura crocea tunneyi, Endangered): 29 records, none since 31 Oct 2018, despite rising birdwatching effort. Treat this as a priority for a targeted survey on the Kakadu-region floodplains.

confidence.notes: 416 of 649 statistical-tier taxa had at least 20 located records in both windows; 35 lost at least 30% of their 10 km AOO. Recording effort rose about 1.9× between windows, so contractions run against the effort trend. Many are still driven by a large baseline source dropping out: Victorian Biodiversity Atlas records, NESP compilations ending in 2020, Fauna Atlas N.T., ACT Wildlife Atlas. Re-running on datasets present in both windows removes or reverses the contraction for several of them (olive ridley, snubfin dolphin, Australian humpback dolphin, Lord Howe currawong, squatter pigeon).

input.summary: 35 statistical-tier taxa show a 10 km AOO contraction of at least 30% between 2017–19 and 2022–24, despite roughly doubled recording effort. About a third of these are source artefacts. The contractions that persist on consistent sources are listed individually.

confidence.level: low as evidence of real range growth
confidence.notes: 234 of 416 eligible taxa (56%) expanded by at least 30% in 10 km AOO. This is what a roughly 1.9× rise in all-taxa recording produces without any biological change. The largest expansions come from new survey programmes (e.g. post-2019–20 fire surveys on Kangaroo Island), iNaturalist uptake, and reintroductions (e.g. Bettongia lesueur in managed and NSW reintroduction datasets). Expansions should not be read as recovery without effort correction.

input.summary: 234 statistical-tier taxa show a 10 km AOO expansion of at least 30%, about six times as many as contractions. This is mostly the doubling of recording effort, plus new surveys and reintroductions, not real range growth. Do not cite these as recovery without effort-corrected analysis.

confidence.notes: Record numbers barely changed (1,352 to 1,203) while the 10 km AOO halved, against rising effort. Part of the drop is the Victorian Biodiversity Atlas supplying 493 baseline records and none recently (possibly withheld as sensitive), but using only datasets present in both windows still gives 10,400 to 6,400 km² (−38%). eBird records rose from 285 to 792, so birders are concentrating at fewer sites. The bird is nomadic.

input.summary: Regent honeyeater (Critically Endangered): 10 km AOO fell 49% (12,600 to 6,400 km²) and EOO 78% between 2017–19 and 2022–24, on similar record numbers. The contraction holds (−38%) on consistent sources. This is the strongest contraction signal among high-profile birds, and the missing Victorian records should be sought.

confidence.notes: The Victorian Biodiversity Atlas fell from 350 to 4 records, which drives much of the fall in records. On consistent sources the AOO goes from 9,400 to 6,600 km² (−30%, borderline). The baseline EOO of 1.59 million km² is implausible for this subspecies and indicates outlying or mislocated baseline records, so the EOO change should be ignored.

input.summary: South-eastern red-tailed black-cockatoo (Endangered): 10 km AOO fell 33% (9,800 to 6,600 km²), but this mostly reflects Victorian atlas records drying up. On consistent sources the change is borderline (−30%). Get the recovery team's count data before acting; the EOO change is an artefact of outlying baseline records.

confidence.notes: Records collapsed from 1,169 to 86, almost entirely because ACT Wildlife Atlas monitoring records fell from 1,140 to 40, so this is largely a reporting change. Consistent sources still show 1,900 to 1,100 km² (−42%). BioNet contributed 34 new recent records. The baseline EOO of over 600,000 km² suggests mislocated records.

input.summary: Tympanocryptis lineata (Critically Endangered): 10 km AOO halved (2,300 to 1,100 km²) and is still down 42% on consistent sources. The main driver is that ACT Wildlife Atlas monitoring records fell from 1,140 to 40, so ask ACT for current monitoring data before interpreting.

NSW BioNet rose from 667 to 1,090. Consistent sources give −31%. The fall in Victoria is probably reporting, not loss; the NSW and ACT pattern needs separate checking.

input.summary: Purple-wood wattle (Acacia carneorum, Vulnerable): 10 km AOO down 69% and EOO down 91%, and the contraction holds on consistent sources. This is one of the more robust contractions and justifies resurvey of 2017–19 stands in western NSW.

confidence.notes: AOO contracts on consistent sources (1,900 to 300 km²), but EOO grew, so recent records are scattered over a wider area. The baseline was dominated by a 2017 BioNet survey pulse on the NSW North Coast, a bioregion that is silent since (157 baseline records). A survey-pulse artefact is likely.

input.summary: Booroolong frog (Endangered): 10 km AOO down 30% and 2 km AOO down 66% on unchanged sources, with the NSW North Coast silent since 2021. This is a credible contraction signal, so prioritise stream surveys at former 2017–19 sites.

confidence.notes: Records under this subspecies name fell from 137 to 31, almost all because Queensland WildNet dropped from 126 to 5. EOO is stable. Most birders record godwits at species level, so subspecies-labelled records depend on a few sources. Probably a labelling or reporting artefact.

confidence.notes: Fauna Atlas N.T. supplied 6,138 baseline records and 24 recent (source ends 2024-03). Nearly half the recent records (96 of 206) are from managed AWC sites. The 2 km AOO and EOO both increased.

confidence.notes: 747 of 774 baseline records come from the NESP A12 compilation, which ends in 2020. No dataset contributes to both windows. EOO increased about fourfold.

WITH s AS (SELECT o.record_id, o.taxon_concept_id, o.ibra_region, o.geom, (o.event_date AT TIME ZONE 'Australia/Sydney')::date d, o.data_resource_uid, o.coordinate_uncertainty_m u
 FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences o JOIN corpus.taxon_tiers t USING (taxon_concept_id)
 WHERE t.statistical_tier AND (o.event_date AT TIME ZONE 'Australia/Sydney')::date BETWEEN '2026-09-01' AND '2026-09-30'),
p AS (SELECT o.taxon_concept_id, o.ibra_region, o.geom, (o.event_date AT TIME ZONE 'Australia/Sydney')::date d
 FROM corpus.analysable_occurrences o WHERE o.taxon_concept_id IN (SELECT taxon_concept_id FROM s) AND (o.event_date AT TIME ZONE 'Australia/Sydney')::date BETWEEN '2015-01-01' AND '2026-09-30'),
m AS (SELECT taxon_concept_id, count(*) n1519, count(*) FILTER (WHERE extract(month FROM d)=9) n_sep FROM p WHERE d <= '2019-12-31' GROUP BY 1),
f AS (SELECT s.*,
  NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM p WHERE p.taxon_concept_id=s.taxon_concept_id AND p.d < s.d AND ST_DWithin(p.geom::geography, s.geom::geography, 100000)) far,
  (s.ibra_region IS NOT NULL AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM p WHERE p.taxon_concept_id=s.taxon_concept_id AND p.d < s.d AND p.ibra_region=s.ibra_region)) newreg,
  coalesce(m.n1519 >= 100 AND m.n_sep < 0.01*m.n1519, false) offseason, m.n1519, m.n_sep
 FROM s LEFT JOIN m USING (taxon_concept_id)),
n AS (SELECT f.*, (SELECT ST_Distance(p.geom::geography, f.geom::geography) FROM p WHERE p.taxon_concept_id=f.taxon_concept_id AND p.d < f.d ORDER BY p.geom::geography <-> f.geom::geography LIMIT 1)/1000 dist_km
 FROM f WHERE far OR newreg OR offseason)
SELECT tx.scientific_name, tx.national_status, n.ibra_region, count(*) recs, bool_or(far) far, bool_or(newreg) newreg, bool_or(offseason) offseason,
 round(max(dist_km)::numeric,1) max_dist_km, max(n1519) n1519, max(n_sep) n_sep, string_agg(DISTINCT data_resource_uid, ',') ds, round(max(u)::numeric) max_unc, min(d)::text first_d, n.taxon_concept_id
FROM n JOIN corpus.taxa tx USING (taxon_concept_id) GROUP BY tx.scientific_name, tx.national_status, n.ibra_region, n.taxon_concept_id
ORDER BY bool_or(far) DESC, bool_or(newreg) DESC, max(dist_km) DESC

content.text:
I've recorded 97 insights for the September 2026 report, each based on queries I ran. One thing to know first: September 2026 data are nearly all from one source. Only 3 datasets have loaded any records for the month, against 34 in September 2024. iNaturalist supplies 2,861 of the 3,199 threatened-species records and NSW BioNet a partial 336. eBird, Birdata, the other state atlases and managed-site monitoring haven't arrived yet.

I counted dates in Australian local time; on the raw UTC timestamps the silent count is 377 instead of 376.

## 1. Silent species (Oct 2023 – Sep 2026): 3 headlines and 45 individual cases
- **Silent:** 376 of 1,852 taxa have no record in the window, 123 of them Critically Endangered. 313 of the 376 were already data-poor (fewer than 10 records since 2015).
- **Evidence gap:** 635 taxa (178 Critically Endangered) have fewer than 10 records since 2015. Several closely managed species are almost absent from ALA: southern corroboree frog and Baw Baw frog have 1 record each, Gilbert's potoroo 3, western swamp turtle 7. Their monitoring data aren't reaching ALA.
- **Regional silence:** 184 taxon–bioregion pairs (130 taxa, 65 bioregions). In 88 of them, all the 2015–2019 records come from one dataset, usually a one-off survey.
- **Cases worth acting on:**
  - Illawarra Irene was recorded every year 2016–2022 and not since.
  - The Carpentarian rock-rat and the Alligator Rivers yellow chat have had no records since 2017 and 2018.
  - The regent honeyeater has gone unrecorded in the New England Tablelands although recording effort there rose.
  - The striated grasswren (subspecies *howei*) has had no record at its only Riverina site since 2019, while recording there stayed high.
- **Probably not real loss:**
  - The northern river shark, dwarf sawfish and speartooth shark went silent when the NESP research datasets ended in 2019–2020.
  - Several NT mammal silences come from Fauna Atlas N.T. (last record March 2024) and from surveys ending.
  - The 507 Sydney Basin records of the southern bent-wing bat look like a naming error.

## 2. Range change (2017–19 vs 2022–24): 2 headlines and 15 individual taxa
- 416 of the 649 statistical-tier taxa had enough records in both windows. 35 contracted and 234 expanded.
- All-species recording rose 1.9× between the windows, so most expansions reflect more effort, new surveys or reintroductions, not real growth.
- I re-ran each contraction using only datasets present in both windows, to check whether it holds up:
  - **Holds up:** regent honeyeater (−49% overall, −38% on consistent sources), purple-wood wattle (−69%) and Booroolong frog (−30% on unchanged sources).
  - **Driven by a source stopping:** olive ridley turtle and snubfin dolphin. The northern brushtail possum, golden sun moth and *Tympanocryptis lineata* fell mostly because NT, Victorian and ACT atlas records dried up.
- The burrowing bettong's expansion is entirely managed or reintroduced animals. 8,265 of its recent records are in NSW BioNet, which is tagged as a wild dataset, so they can inflate wild trends.

## 3. Notable records (September 2026): 30 of 41 groups recorded
All notable records are from iNaturalist.
- **Worth verifying:**
  - A greater bilby report in the Gascoyne, 552 km from any record since 2015, and another in a new bioregion (Murchison) the next day.
  - A Mertens' water monitor 230 km from prior records.
  - A common greenshank at Lake Eyre.
  - A spectacled flying-fox found during a mass flying-fox rescue (about 70 animals in two weeks). Queensland wildlife health contacts should be alerted.
- **Likely errors:** a brush-tailed rabbit-rat in Victoria, 2,742 km from any prior record; macadamia and magenta lilly pilly records that are probably planted trees; and a *Seringia exastia* record whose location uncertainty (102 km) is larger than its distance from prior records (101 km).

## Other (2 insights)
- The September 2026 reporting lag described above.
- The end of the NT and NESP research datasets has left northern mammals, sharks, sawfish and coastal dolphins with almost no current data.

Three summary statements rest on general knowledge rather than my queries:
- That the Norfolk Island robin and the southern bent-wing bat don't occur where the records place them.
- The Kermadec petrel's single site is described as the Lord Howe group; the data only give the Pacific Subtropical Islands bioregion.
- Arthraxon hispidus's two silent bioregions are called its northern NSW strongholds.

I can't edit recorded insights, so check those three wordings if anything rests on them.
